replying_to: Replying to Regarding baselines and Figure 9

content.title: Re: Regarding baselines and figure 9
content.comment:
Thank you for the interesting question. Indeed, if we should assume that Baydin et al.+averaging (+single meta lr, which by definition is part of Baydin et al.) *could* be combined with a single workable hyperparameter configuration, that would hypothetically be optimal over any workload and constant regardless of the dataset at hand, then the proposed method (efficient SGD-TLR / sgd_tlr) would have little added-value over this setting. We argue that a) such a setting cannot exist, and that meta-learning rate is indeed a critical hyperparameter, b) the strength of our method lies in exactly that we do not need to bother fine-tuning meta-lr over the workload at hand. According to our method, the step we need to take for adjusting learning rate is automatically tuned in each iteration, theoretically justified, and following the updates shown in-text. 

We apologize and thank you for pointing out the erratum in Figure 9 concerning the y-axis; we have fixed this (see below). Figure 9 serves to support our claim that the required meta-learning rate is indeed a critical hyperparameter. We agree that despite showing this sensitivity, it is not clear how our method (sgd_tlr) compares to a “good” setting of this hyper-parameter. To better understand the performance of the fixed meta-lr variation (Baydin et al.+averaging) that we explore in Fig.9, we provide the curves of our method along with the reported ones and a scaled version of the axes in the following anonymized gdrive link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CHJNAt8c1PWIzgMc0fUQF3d8aiwKVx7m/view?usp=sharing \
Please note that we have added a new curve for sgd_tlr, comparing it to the variants that require a fixed meta-lr. Therein it is shown that our method has better overall behavior across all settings, in the sense that our method attains a better result faster and much more consistently than the other settings (for example, meta-lr=0.1 is oscillating wildly between good and very bad loss/acc values).

Concerning the idea of choosing a default meta-learning rate value, one can say that $\eta=0.01$ works well enough for the scenarios presented in Fig.9 (at least for CIFAR10/100; in MNIST this isn’t optimal). However, this observation cannot be generalized because the reported behavior corresponds to a specific initial learning rate ($a_0=0.1$). Changing the initial learning rate can lead to different $\eta$ requirements, as this extra figure shows (anonymized gdrive link) for $a_0=0.01$: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cjsNfUl5P4z4GONob_-_Cvl21uSpjfd5/view?usp=sharing \
For example, in this setting of $a_0=0.01$, $\eta=0.01$ leads to an oscillating behavior and suboptimal performance. (A minor, yet interesting, observation is that large values of $\eta$, such as 0.1, may lead to intense oscillations that resemble a restarting tactic and can achieve “unstable” solutions of very good accuracy).

These results suggest (perhaps not surprisingly) that the choice of an optimal meta-lr is strongly correlated to other hyperparameters, as well as the characteristics of the dataset / problem at hand. We interpret this conclusion as an advantage of our method, which integrates a mechanism that in effect computes an optimal meta-step and furthermore fine-tunes it in each iteration for practically negligible cost.

Concerning our method, let us clarify that we did not select an "optimized" averaging hyperparameter. Figure 6 only reports the effect of this hyper-parameter to our algorithm, since we had stated $p=⅓$ as our default value in the main text (e.g. the case of $p=0.5$ has a higher end accuracy in the example of Fig. 6).

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for the additional plots, but they still aren't fully addressing the reviewers concerns. You've tuned an update rule that (alpha_t < 1.25 alpha_{t+1}) which is independent of the second order term. A similar rule seems like it could fix Baydin et. al. particularly given the unstable Baydin runs have the learned lr jump quickly.

It is really easy, particularly when you are running all of your own baselines to tweak a method to make it look good (this is how our community has managed to publish 100 Adam variants that don't actually outperform Adam). What reviewers are asking for is a good faith effort to look for a single stable Baydin et. al. configuration that works on the considered baselines (you spent some considerable effort to find a good configuration of your method on the considered baselines, as evident in the choices of p, a_0 and c).


"Concerning our method, let us clarify that we did not select an "optimized" averaging hyperparameter. Figure 6 only reports the effect of this hyper-parameter to our algorithm, since we had stated ⅓ as our default value in the main text (e.g. the case of  has a higher end accuracy in the example of Fig. 6)." The fact that p=0.5 is the best on one workload isn't really relevant here, because you are arguing that your method works "ok" on diverse workloads without needed to be tuned for workloads individually. If we only care about optimizing a single workload's performance, it's very likely SGD with a well tuned schedule would match/outperform all considered methods you present.

"Concerning the idea of choosing a default meta-learning rate value, one can say that  works well enough for the scenarios presented in Fig.9 (at least for CIFAR10/100; in MNIST this isn’t optimal). However, this observation cannot be generalized because the reported behavior corresponds to a specific initial learning rate ()." This doesn't really answer the question on whether or not Baydin et. al. can be tuned to do well on most of the considered workloads. The fact that Figure 9 found a configuration that matches your method on 2/3 and is close on the third does beg the question.

content.title: Final Comment
content.comment:
We are thankful for the overall feedback, providing valuable insights about the presentation of the experimental results.  We respectfully disagree with the deduction "you spent some considerable effort to find a good configuration of your method on the considered baselines, as evident in the choices of p, a_0 and c". The comment "If we only care about optimizing a single workload's performance, it's very likely SGD with a well tuned schedule would match/outperform all considered methods you present" is in line with our main point. We do not state in any case that the proposed algorithm could outperform a carefully tuned optimizer+scheduler, rather that we propose a robust enough approach w.r.t. hyper-parameters that can swiftly provide well-performing solutions. Moreover, from our perspective, the advantages over Baydin et al. are straightforward: we impose a better, more stable behavior to the learning rate development through the use of second order information. Apart from the theoretical benefit of such a Newton formulation, the experimental results (along with the extra presented Figures) show exactly this acclaimed robustness, contrary to the simpler case of Baydin et al., where different settings lead to different behaviors. Of course, if we choose a specific fine-tuned meta learning-rate per initial hyper-parameters/datasets/models we will achieve similar behavior, similar to the case of a fine-tuned scheduling tactic.
 
As an extra observation, the reported bound has an entirely different motivation in our formulation compared to the case of the first-order derivative. Specifically, in our formulation the bound is used to prevent an exploding increase of the learning rate in the initial stage of the proposed algorithm due to the possibility of the denominator being close to zero.  To this end we selected a rather restricting bound in order to be sure that such exploding behavior is not met. We considered that such a bound is not optimal and a dynamic bound would further improve the behavior of our algorithm. However, this bound is not responsible for stopping the oscillations in our algorithm, since the decreasing learning rate stage has an entirely different expression, resembling an exponential decay compared to the behavior of Baydin et al. which may lead to a rapidly decreasing learning rate. Applying a similar bound to the first-order case (Baydin et al.) will cut off entirely the oscillations and simply stop the whole procedure since the learning rate is zero-ed when it becomes negative, but it will not be advantageous for the whole procedure apart from terminating oscillations (note that "small" oscillations may be helpful). This can be seen in the following figures where the same bound was used (anonymized links): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1zqBJqE3DpPHF05i-tL9a93d9lvF66gtt/view?usp=sharing ,  https://drive.google.com/file/d/16CXPXnMkfg-kimPHVd4Ia8q0EhA6akyr/view?usp=sharing .

content.title: Paper Decision
content.comment:
The work presents a modification to existing approaches of automatic learning rate adaptation (called TLR) via a second order approximation of the function mapping step size to the change in loss when optimized with SGD. This was easily the most controversial paper in the AC's stack, with 4 reviewers advocating accept and 2 reviewers strongly arguing for reject. The authors also went through considerable effort to address reviewer and AC concerns and uploaded multiple additional experiments and ablations to support the robustness and efficacy of the proposed method. Despite a long discussion and rebuttal period, reviewers were unable to reach a consensus. There were several different aspects of the work whose merits were thoroughly debated during the rebuttal period.

The first aspect regarded what the exact contribution of the work was. Initial reviewers who were very high on the work believed that the entire derivation from equation (1) to equation (9) was novel. However, as other reviewers correctly pointed out (1) to (7) is a standard derivation of adaptive learning rates and has appeared in several prior works. Instead it is primarily equation (9) that is the contribution. Given that multiple reviewers initially believed that (1 -> 7) was a novel contribution, I feel it is safe to say that the authors do not adequately discuss their contributions with respect to prior work. However, all reviewers in the end agreed that equation (9) is novel and potentially interesting (though some remain skeptical of it's utility).

The second topic of debate regarded the short horizon bias raised by reviewer hkZ3. The short horizon bias presents a fundamental barrier to meta optimization of the learning rate. To summarize, greedily selecting the step size to minimize the loss will result in the optimizer taking too small of steps in the flat directions of an ill conditioned loss surface. This results in faster training in the short term but slower training in the long run. The presented method seeks to greedily optimize the loss over short time scales and thus will be subject to the short horizon bias. The initial draft of the work did not include any discussion of this prior work. During the rebuttal, the authors initially argued that their method can help mitigate the short horizon bias before later concluding that it is a limitation of the method. There was debate between the AC and reviewers regarding whether or not existing methods of adaptive learning rate schedules were already at a fundamental barrier presented by the short horizon bias. One reviewer even mentioned that in their own research they have abandoned the general approach of adaptive learning rates because they cannot overcome this issue. This debate was never resolved, it's plausible to the AC that there is room for increasing the robustness of existing approaches while not addressing the short horizon issue. It is the AC's opinion however that the work would be significantly strengthened with experiments directly addressing the short horizon issue.

The final item of debate regarded the strength of the considered baselines. The authors claim that the second order term in (eq 9) largely removes the need for tuning relative to Baydin et. al. and that the method outperforms multiple baselines across multiple workloads, including Adam (Kingma et. al.), SLS (Vaswani et. al.), and SPS (Loizou et. al.). Indeed multiple plots are given showing that the authors have found a configuration of their method that consistently outperforms certain fixed configurations of the considered baselines. Furthermore, ablations are presented which suggest that indeed it is the addition of equation (9) that is responsible for this strong performance. Despite all of this presented evidence some reviewers remained skeptical, and believed that they could produce a different but fixed configuration of say Baydin et. al. (or even Adam) which matched the proposed method on all of the considered workloads. There are compelling reasons for reviewers to consider the presented experiments with skepticism. Indeed the deep learning optimization literature has for years struggled to make progress despite publishing hundreds of papers---see for example the results of [1] which perform an independent comparison of 100's of published methods and found that none convincingly outperform Adam. Given this, it is clear that the current standard for evaluating optimizers in the literature is inadequate if we are to reliably make progress.

To give a more relevant example of the difficulty of comparing optimization methods, suppose for the sake of argument that we were not evaluating the efficacy of TLR but instead the method of Vaswani et. al. (SLS). Vaswani et. al. makes many similar claims as the proposed method, namely the method consistently outperforms Adam across multiple workloads and enjoys a similar robustness to hyperparameters (e.g. their Figure 6). However, in Figure 3 and 4 of this work we see SLS no longer outperforms Adam on the considered workloads. If Vaswani et. al. had argued for acceptance based on the author's Figure 3 and 4, I don't think any reviewer would have recommended acceptance. This begs the obvious question, why does SLS consistently outperform Adam in the experiments run by Vaswani et. al., but not in the experiments run in the considered paper? There are at least two possible answers here, both of which are concerning. Either Vaswani et. al. is yet another method that generally doesn't outperform Adam or in comparing SLS with TLR in this work the authors did not properly tune SLS in their baselines. Furthermore, what is going to happen if future work tries to compare against TLR? Will TLR still look better than Adam or will independent review find that TLR is yet another method that on average performs about as well as Adam? As a reviewer trying to compare the two papers I see very similar evidence given supporting the two methods and thus I am left with an unresolved contradiction.

Given all of this, I am forced to conclude that there is insufficient evidence presented in this work that the proposed method generally outperforms related methods such as SLS and Adam. A natural question thus is, what would have been sufficient evidence? Indeed the presented experiments seem to be about as convincing as what is shown in previous published methods such as SLS. In a sense the AC is also arguing that Vaswani et. al. presented insufficient evidence that SLS generally outperforms Adam (looking at Figure 3 and 4 perhaps SLS in fact isn't as useful as Vaswani et. al. claim). In looking at the experiments presented in this work, related prior works, and the 100's of methods considered in [1] a common recurring theme is that when comparing with prior work authors consistently run their own implementation of baselines on workloads of their choosing, rather than directly comparing with published results. In doing so, this leaves open the question regarding whether or not the authors (perhaps inadvertently!) are only considering workloads and hyperparameter settings which favor their own method rather than giving a realistic assessment of the efficacy of their own methods relative to others. Thus, if the authors wish to argue that TLR generally outperforms SLS, a strong piece of evidence the authors could provide is to run TLR directly on the open sourced code provided by Vaswani et. al. Show the reviewer how TLR compares when added directly to (for example) Vaswani et. al. Figure 4. In doing so, the authors will have addressed any concerns reviewers may have about how well represented SLS is, as the authors will be comparing against SLS in a setting where there were actual incentives to make SLS look good.

1. Schmidt et. al. Descending in a crowded valley – Benchmarking Deep Learning Optimizers, https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01547
